full_judgment:
Latifur Rahman, J.: This Rule at the instance of the defendants-petitioners is directed against the order of Subordinate Judge, 3rd Court, Dhaka in Miscellaneous Case No. 937 of 1981 allowing an application under Order 9, Rule 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure and restoring the suit to its original file and number. 

 2. The plaintiff-opposite party filed a suit for partition. The suit was fixed for hearing on 3.8.76 and in the meanwhile the records were called for and the records came before this court in F.A. No. 226 of 1974. After the return of the records from the High Court the plaintiff was not informed about the date. Neither the Advocate of the petitioner nor the lawyer's clerk was intimated about the date of hearing and the case was dismissed on 3.1.78. The plaintiff having come to know on 5.7.79 about the dismissal order filed the application for restoration of the suit. According to the plaintiff he was prevented by sufficient cause for not appearing in the case after the transmission of the records from the High Court as the date of hearing was not intimated to the lawyer and his clerk. The plaintiff opposite party suffered irreparable loss and hence the case for restoration, 

 5. Mr. Serajur Rahman, the learned Advocate appearing for the opposite party submits that in the facts of present case, Article 181 of the Limitation Act will apply as the default occurred primarily due to the fault of the court and for no fault of the petitioner and for securing the ends of justice the application should be treated as one under section 151 of the Code. 

 6. From the impugned order it appears that the plaintiff examined two witnesses and the defendant did not examine any witness. Further, the court found as a matter of fact, that the original suit was fixed for hearing on 3.8.76 and the records of the case were transmitted to the High Court on 28.4.76 in connection with F. A. No. 226 of 1974. Thereafter, the records were received back by the trial court on 13.5.77. On that date the court fixed 14.6.77 for S.D. and directed the office to inform both sides. On 14.6.77 the court again directed to inform the learned Advocate as the learned Advocates were not informed earlier as per the order of the Court. We have perused the order-sheets of the court and the findings in the impugned order are borne out by the order sheet. Thus, it is correct to say that the learned Advocate for the plaintiff-opposite party was not informed about the arrival of the records from the High Court in spite of the order of the trial Court. In such circumstances, the suit which was fixed for hearing on 3.1.78 was dismissed for default as no step was taken. 

 7. In the background of this positive finding and observations as made in the impugned order, we are to see whether the submission of the learned Advocate for the petitioner is tenable in law and fact. It is a fact that the application under Order 9, rule 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure was filed within 30 days from the date of knowledge and not within 30 days from the date of dismissal as specified in Article 163 of the Limitation Act. In the present case, the application was filed admittedly 1 year and 6 months alter the dismissal order and the court considered that in the facts of the present case that limitation will run from 30 days from the date of knowledge. 

 9. Before answering this question, we like to observe that if the application under Order 9, rule 9 of the Code would have been filed along with s. 151 of the Code then certainly the court could have restored the case for the ends of justice or to prevent abuse of the process of the court. This application was filed only under Order 9, rule 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure but the broad fact remains that due to default of the court's officer the matter was never brought to the notice of the Advocate as ordered by the court and in such circumstances, the court restored the case holding that the question of limitation in this present case is to be decided from the date of knowledge. It is not disputed that a court has inherent jurisdiction to restore a suit which has been dismissed for default owing to the mistake of the court itself or owing to the mistake of the court's officer for doing real and substantial justice. 

 10. It is true that in an application under Order 9, rule 9 of the Code, Article 163 of the Limitation Act will apply and the court cannot grant extension of time. But in the facts of the present case we can easily treat the application as one under Order 9, rule 9 read with section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure, Section 151 of the Code does not make any mention of the time within which the court may exercise its power under section 151 of the Code. 

 11. In the present case the court found its own fault and restored the case to its file and number. In such a case even on an application suo motu the court could have restored the suit for doing ex Milo justiciae under the inherent power of the court. If we accept the contention of the learned Advocate for the petitioner it will amount to that in a litigation where a party is kept in ignorance due to the fault of the court or officers of the court, even then the Litigant is devoid of any remedial action. We are afraid such a narrow interpretation cannot be given for securing the substantial ends of justice for which the court exits. Article 181 of the Limitation Act reads as follows:- 

 Thus, in the facts of the present case we are of view that three years limitation will run in the present case and the present case will be governed under Article 181 of the Limitation Act and not Article 163 of the Act as submitted by the learned Advocate for the petitioner. 

 12. Before parting with the case, it is to be stated that the relief one can seek under section 115 is a discretionary relief and if the court has committed any error of law but that has not resulted in a decision occasioning a failure of justice, then the court may not exercise the discretion under section 115 of the Code, but if there is an error of law but no substantial injustice has been caused, this court may not interfere in revision, Consequently, the submissions raised by the learned Advocate for the petitioner fails. The impugned order thus has not caused any failure of justice. 

 Let the records be sent down forthwith. Let the trial Court decide the case as expeditiously as possible.
